study type: Secondary analysis of a prospective study with cross-sectional analysis
exposure: Operative vaginal delivery attempted by attending obstetricians
second-stage pushing phase longer than 30 minutes
persistent occiput posterior or transverse positions
level of experience of obstetrician (resident vs attending)
Operative vaginal delivery attempted by residents under supervision
outcome: Severe maternal morbidity (defined as third- or fourth-degree perineal laceration, perineal hematoma, cervical laceration, extended uterine incision for cesareans, postpartum hemorrhage >1500 mL, surgical hemostatic procedures, uterine artery embolization, blood transfusion, infection, thromboembolic events, admission to the intensive care unit, or maternal death)

Severe neonatal morbidity (defined as a 5-minute Apgar score <7, umbilical artery pH <7.00, need for resuscitation or intubation, neonatal trauma, intraventricular hemorrhage greater than grade 2, neonatal intensive care unit admission for more than 24 hours, convulsions, sepsis, or neonatal death)
cohort: 2192 women with live singleton term fetuses in vertex presentation who underwent an attempted operative vaginal delivery in a tertiary care university hospital
finding: Management of attempted operative vaginal deliveries by residents under the supervision of attending obstetricians, compared with by the attending obstetricians themselves, did not appear to be associated with either an increase in maternal or neonatal morbidity.
